extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and professionals interested in news production, media sociology, and journalism practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and conceptual dimensions for how news is produced, selected, framed, and circulated within news organizations (drawing on ethnographic observation of TV and newspaper newsrooms). Useful for evaluating newsworthiness, newsroom routines, and the institutional role of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: News is a window on the world. Through its frame, Americans learn of themselves and others, of their own institutions, leaders, and life styles ... The view through a window depends upon whether the window is large or small, has many panes or few, whether the glass is opaque or clear, whether the window faces a street or a backyard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the window/frame metaphor: frame size, panes, opacity, and vantage point determine what is visible and salient. The chapter emphasizes examining how that frame is constituted—how organizations of newswork and newsworkers create the frame via routines, professional norms, and organizational structures. Implication: evaluate news by asking how framing choices (space, perspective, emphasis) shape public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness: pertinence to speaker and listener
rubrics_metrics.description: Items must be judged pertinent to both speaker and listener in order to be judged newsworthy and must somehow present themselves to the speaker in the course of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the professor's 'three green lights' vs the story about 'Joe'—both are particulars, but only the one judged mutually pertinent becomes 'news.' When evaluating whether an occurrence becomes news, ask whether it is pertinent to intended audiences and whether transmitter and receiver share interest/recognition. Scoring note: pertinence is socially negotiated, not purely objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial and temporal purview of reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: How can particulars embedded in strips of ongoing activity come into the reporter’s spatial and temporal purview?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters only can report what enters their temporal/spatial reach. Evaluate newsgathering by tracing how events enter reporters' view (beats, assignments, press rooms, chance encounters). Examples: private conversations (president/provost) or distant happenings may be outside reporters' purview and therefore not covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge embedded in stratification systems (access limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are some items not related because knowledge is embedded in stratification systems?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power hierarchies and social stratification determine access to information (e.g., ordinary people cannot access what elites discuss privately). When assessing coverage gaps, consider which actors are spatially or institutionally excluded from reporters' access. Example: professor could not report president/provost talks; reporters lack equal access to all sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taken-for-granted routines and professional assumptions lead to omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are some items not noticed because they are taken for granted as aspects of the social world (professional skills, routine meeting placements, common background assumptions)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine features of organizational life or occupational competence are often omitted from news because they are assumed. Evaluators should consider what is invisible due to professional familiarity (e.g., meeting procedures, assumed knowledge) and how that shapes what is reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as an institutional ally of legitimated institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: News is an ally of legitimated institutions. The secretary of state can float an idea in the news media; the 'average' man or woman does not have such access to the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the relational role of media: news organizations are embedded in institutional networks and can serve institutional actors (e.g., to trial balloons or coordinate responses). Evaluate whose interests are facilitated by coverage and how media access privileges official or legitimated voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting function
rubrics_metrics.description: By seeking to disseminate information that people want, need, and should know, news organizations both circulate and shape knowledge ... the news media play an important role in the news consumers' setting of a political agenda. Those topics given the most coverage by the news media are likely to be the topics audiences identify as the most pressing issues of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical measures of coverage volume and placement to evaluate agenda-setting effects. Example citations: McCombs and Shaw. Scoring guidance: more frequent/prominent coverage predicts greater public salience, though causality may be complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: News shapes public explanations and language
rubrics_metrics.description: The news media's explanations of events may serve as the context in which news consumers debate the meaning of events ... e.g., Seattle residents adopted media-offered explanations as an exhaustive list; young men who refused Vietnam service called 'evaders' (media's term) rather than 'resisters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just whether an event is covered, but which explanatory frames and labels are offered. Label choice affects public perception and political orientation; media-provided causal accounts can become taken-for-granted explanatory repertoires among audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and organizational needs shape news practice (profession serves organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: News professional practices serve organizational needs. Professionalism has developed in conjunction with modern news organizations, and professional practices serve organizational needs. Both, in turn, serve to legitimate the status quo, complementing one another's reinforcement of contemporary social arrangements, even as they occasionally compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news workers' decisions, consider organizational logics (deadlines, staffing, ownership, corporate interests) that shape professional norms. Conflicts between reporters and management exist but are conditioned by organizational imperatives; thus professionalism often preserves organizational and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and selection as the core evaluative act
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing is what editors are for and editing is the choice and selection of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of news should foreground editorial selection choices—what to include, exclude, and emphasize. Evaluate headlines, leads, placement, and the selective omission of details as central to meaning construction. Anti-pattern: treating news as a transparent 'reflection' of events rather than a set of editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making news is a negotiated enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Making news is a negotiated enterprise. Both speakers and listeners (and within organizations, reporters, editors, and sources) actively participate in constructing what becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (parent-child, professor-spouse, newsroom interactions) to analyze how negotiation among parties determines story content. Evaluate interactions among sources, reporters, and gatekeepers to see how negotiation shapes which particulars become public.

rubrics_metrics.name: News transforms occurrences into publicly discussable events (public character)
rubrics_metrics.description: News imparts to occurrences their public character as it transforms mere happenings into publicly discussable events ... news as the modern replacement of the town crier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether and how coverage turns private happenings into public issues, enabling coordination, mobilization, or policy responses. Consider the role of naming, locating, and contextualizing events in conferring publicness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative conventions and the claim to factuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythic and news stories are both stories; the news lead proclaims that what follows is factual and hard-nosed, a veridical account of events in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the narrative devices (leads, chronology, sourcing) used to legitimate factual claims. Compare news conventions with other story forms to reveal how narrative structure is used to assert authority and truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints and resources of newswork (organizational context)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a study of the constraints of newswork and of the resources available to newsworkers ... a study of newsworkers as professionals and of newspapers and television newsrooms as complex organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newsroom output in light of organizational resources (staff size, technology, program schedules, ownership, beats). The field-site descriptions (TV station, local daily, NY pressroom) illustrate how differing resources and routines affect what gets covered and how.
